items.title: The Afterlife Is Having a Flea Market
items.summary: He Comes With a Lynchian Flashlight “We’re like lightbulbs. If bliss starts growing inside you, it’s like a light; it affects the environment.” – David Lynch When the flea market locks its doors on Zion Road, the locals rock on porches wrapped around by moonlight. Straight through midnight he floateth down perennial on a two-lane in black patent tapshoes unscuffed by traction. Straight from the level of Eternal Phenomenal he learned from Florentine Christmas card angels, from the final decision of far gone untangled future thought patterns the messenger angel flies from the great director in an antique jacket of black brocade. It spells The Almighty Remarkable across his back embroidered in curlicued letters like Elvis’s latter-day sparkle. He brings an annual and promo greeting only to those on the list from Zion Road the chosen who filled out in fountain pen the questionnaire Are You Saved from a neighbor a lover of sparrows who was finally strangled for asking. Every summer he saileth down and tasteth the precious stones of the Revelation in his beloved’s garden: The jasper sapphire chalcedony emerald sardonyx that bloodlike savor the sardius chrysolite beryl gain favor topaz chrysopraysus earn his whispery praises the jacinth and amethyst swallowed in phases. His earthbound sweetheart strokes her balcony as the pink floribunda roses climb the lattice. She offers up the sacred and the stolen glass tumbler wrapped in motel parchment that is watermarked S A N I T I Z E D. His own tongue recalls the ecstatic whiff of earthly water chlorinized. He removes the epidermal crackle vegetal pale as John the Baptist’s hollow locust shell. Beneath his single Everbrite beam he deciphers the message on the paperskin that protects the nearly immaculate conception, the message only visible to him: Hello people with brains channeled like underground rivers as you search eternal aisles with no direction to find the little batteries to place inside your own heads so you won’t always be lost somewhere in the hardware section. Green Lamp Ghost Beside the Vaseline globe a likewise emerald face a ghost relaxes his salt-and-pepper head bends as he reads from the green-stamp light. I cannot tell the other flea marketers. They’d never haunt a living room with it although I’m sure he will not reappear. How do I know? It might be hard to tell but first of all, I will be looking now. If he isn’t there, I will imagine him and imagining a ghost is never right. They have to come before suspicion peaks, traveling faster than wave or particle and if you try and pull them out of air they will be gone before they ever come. The Message of the Lost Handle “the only thing good is the world’s smallest man who happened to be a personal friend of mine” – Frank Stanford I have set up my vagabond stage in the blue gravel parking lot at the flea market on Zion Road. As the daughter of the world’s smallest man I climb on spider gauze I spin into heaven. My true believers cry upward and they sigh Oh the futility for what the angels might give me. I have climbed up through the wispy to reach at last a big round silver thing and receive the miracle gift from Gabriel’s hands. Sliding back down to my acolytes who follow me from town to town, in the distance I see two dozen yellow school buses parked in rows. All come to the midsouth fair to see my cousins the beautiful hermaphrodites. A crowd gathers around me frowning at my holy grail, a used popcorn popper too shoddy to even donate to the Goodwill. Under the cracked plastic bubble top a few grains of salt remain with the dud kernels petrified by time immemorial. Out falls a transparent yellow tensile handle to something that is gone. On its underside is a raised diagram an old sigil worried down by the hands of the bossy kitchen angels. I strive to concentrate upon the message of the lost handle. I shout, Turn off that radio! Two jackasses spring down off a tailgate and flip me off. The eyelids of my shrinking audience droop with nearly oceanic pity. They whisper, Don’t take it personal, you’re a decent climber . Once I brought down to Ponca City a mylar birthday balloon gone flabby, a grease-spotted bag of cashews half eaten up by the seraphim and everybody just walked away. Too puffed up to take home this stuff the archangels can’t move in their own yard sale. The old prophets received some dazzlers burning bushes parted oceans seventh seal. Oh my fellow human beings, step this way, step beyond your puny life insurance policies. Take the lamp missing its cord the chipped alabaster piece of junk and channel the offering with common redblood wire. Its light will show how to disconnect the nuclear panel to save the world simply over the counter. If you can take from my knobby hands the dullest knife the flattest inner tube. I cannot tell you what God will have you cut, or how you’ll float a river to the Most High. I guess you’re all too scared to make a move, or like they did to Isaiah, you’ll probably saw me in two for giving you something rough instead of something smooth. items.title: How American Girl Doll Lost Its Way
items.summary: Photographs by Elizabeth Renstrom In the early 1990s, when I was in elementary school, a fancy catalog would arrive in the mailbox of our 1950s split-level in Philadelphia four times a year, and I’d hurry to my room to pore over its elaborate spreads. Tea caddies, Windsor chairs, writing quills, ice-cream churns. We didn’t have any antiques in our home, but the lure of the past was so strong that sometimes my sisters, five and seven years older than me, crammed onto my bed to dog-ear the pages too. Most of all, we looked forward to checking in with the girls arrayed there, whose stories we knew so well: Samantha, Molly, Kirsten, Felicity, Addy, and, later in the decade, Josefina. They were the American Girl dolls, preadolescents just slightly older than me, and I was enthralled by the pictures of their period dresses, tiny school supplies, and exotic waxed lunch foods. My own doll was the farm girl Kirsten Larson, a Swedish immigrant to 1850s Minnesota. She had come in a burgundy box, with a slim book titled Meet Kirsten tucked in beside her. I promptly begged for the five other Kirsten books; the historical-fiction series followed the same pattern for each doll, ushering her through a year’s worth of life events, tailored to her personality and time and place. I remember playing with Kirsten in the backyard and having her trace out symbols in the dirt, just as she did with her new friend, a Dakota girl called Singing Bird, in the second book, Kirsten Learns a Lesson . To have such a doll was to own a whole world and the narratives within it. In my blue-collar neighborhood, we lucky doll owners felt that our Boomer parents had entrusted us with a valuable possession, and they had. When they were first introduced, in 1986, American Girl dolls cost a shocking $68 (roughly $208 today). Almost every Millennial I know who once spent hours with her American Girl doll has kept it, lovingly, into adulthood. The dolls’ hardscrabble backstories piqued curiosity about the past. Kirsten’s best friend died of cholera on the journey from Sweden; Samantha Parkington, the wealthy “Victorian beauty” living in 1904 Westchester County, New York, was an orphan; Molly McIntire’s doctor father was off serving in World War II England. Each doll confronted challenges in her young life that felt at once intimate and unfamiliar. Add well-made accessories and vivid history to the mix, and girlhood acquired an allure that Barbie seemed to bypass on her way to her plastic Dreamhouse. Yet as American Girl’s 40th anniversary arrives, the brand finds itself in something of a midlife crisis. In 1998, Pleasant Rowland, the former teacher and textbook writer who’d dreamed up the dolls, sold Pleasant Company to an unlikely steward: Mattel, the company behind Barbie and her stilettos. A quarter century later, the heyday of preteen devotion to playmates from bygone eras seems like, well, a bygone era. Mattel’s dire balance sheets for the American Girl line confirm that the magic has faded. Might a surge of celebratory attention to the Pleasant Company past be the secret to renewed relevance? It certainly could not be better timed, with the Millennial faithful now in their childbearing—and toy-buying—years. With Rowland’s spare-no-effort ethos of product creation clearly in mind, Mattel has released The Making of American Girl , a chronicle of Pleasant Company’s origin story that resembles the sumptuous catalogs of my childhood, only far grander in scale. The coffee-table book is a canny paean to the dozen years of Rowland’s leadership. Extolling her “courage and conviction,” it dwells on her commitment to craftsmanship. The scrapbook-style spreads showcase mock-ups of her early brainstorming, the fabrics she insisted on, the dovetailed furniture joints and delicate details on all those teeny accessories that girls craved and parents put on their credit cards. Designed as a nostalgia trip for Millennials, it works. My 9- and 4-year-old daughters showed the book off to their playmates one weekend afternoon, but it was those girls’ 40-something mom who lingered over it with me, comparing notes on the expensive items we had known better than to ask for in childhood, such as the bisque plate and mug for Kirsten, made by the renowned Rowe Pottery Works in Wisconsin. But what about the rest of the story of the doll that had become America’s second-most-popular by the late ’90s? That’s left to Amanda FitzSimons, a journalist who did not have the cooperation of Mattel, or of the now-85-year-old Rowland, for her smart and colorful cultural analysis, An American Girl: How a Billion-Dollar Doll and Its Unlikely Founder Changed Girlhood Forever . That means she’s free, after exploring how the dolls and books became unexpected hits, to describe how the American Girl brand’s identity eventually grew so muddled that it has become barely recognizable. FitzSimons starts with Rowland’s big idea, conceived on a trip to Colonial Williamsburg in the early 1980s and transformed into an elaborate business plan over a weekend at her northern-Wisconsin cabin, where the woodstove and outhouse had her thinking about life in the past. The books, “for girls about girls,” came first—they were “the heart of” the American Girl collection, in Rowland’s words. A boss who looked for tenacity in her employees as well as her dolls, Rowland liked to say that her initials, PTR, stood for “Prepare to Redo”; a researcher at the company devoted a day, for example, to conferring with poultry-science experts to determine the exact hour at which Kirsten’s hens would lay eggs. With that attention to detail, Rowland turned the business into a high-volume, high-value sensation. Over time, Pleasant Company offered ever more accessories, such as carefully constructed craft kits (I had my eye on a wooden loom for weaving a doll sash), stationery, and matching outfits for dolls and their girls. But above all, what Rowland sold was the idea that girlhood was important, in need of preservation. Her American Girl enterprise, FitzSimons argues, was a mission to rescue an endangered phase of life. Girlhood was slipping away. The term tween , which encompasses kids as young as 8, was popularized as a marketing tool in the ’80s and quickly became shorthand for a child who didn’t act like a child. Late-20th-century girls, Rowland worried from the start, “turn on the television set and the world comes down on them hard. It’s sexually explicit, it’s dangerous and violent, it’s angry, complaining, discouraging.” By the mid-’90s, the phenomenon of kids aging out of pastimes earlier was well documented. FitzSimons credits Rowland with an astute insight amid rising calls to shore up girls’ self-confidence: “It wasn’t that girls wanted to be older,” she writes; “it was that they wanted to be understood, feel important.” The dolls’ figures never matured, and the books didn’t include periods or crushes; friends, school, and adventure occupied the girls’ imaginations. Samantha fights back when a local menace puts salt in her birthday ice cream; colonial-era Felicity Merriman befriends the daughter of a Loyalist family despite her father’s Revolutionary politics. In aiming to transport girls to other worlds, Rowland had more than innocent fantasy and vivid Americana in mind. Her goal was to encourage play that felt immersive and incorporated historical adversity . The books included plotlines about children working in factories and the displacement of Native people in the Midwest. Her cast expanded to include a second trio of dolls—Felicity, as well as Josefina Montoya , who lives on a New Mexico rancho in 1824, and Addy Walker , an enslaved girl who escapes to 1864 Philadelphia. items.title: The Best Kind of Book Adaptation
items.summary: The couple seated next to me at the Metropolitan Opera’s latest world premiere did not stay for the second act; perhaps they didn’t appreciate the puppeteered genitalia that unfurled onstage shortly after the curtain rose. I understood their alarm. After watching a dress rehearsal a week earlier, I had texted my boyfriend: “I am shocked by the size of Hans Vollman’s puppet penis.” Vollman is one of the central characters in Lincoln in the Bardo , adapted by the composer Missy Mazzoli and the librettist Royce Vavrek from George Saunders’s Booker Prize–winning 2017 novel of the same name . Like almost everyone else in the tale, Vollman is dead but in profound denial about that fact—in his case, because he can’t reckon with the tragedy of having expired before he could consummate his new marriage. Hence the outsize appendage: a perpetual reminder of Vollman’s unfinished business. It may seem puerile for one of the most prominent opera companies in the world to put such effort into illustrating the undignified source of Vollman’s grief. In fact, although the puppet might make audiences laugh—or leave—it’s a striking symbol of why operatic adaptations of literature can be so exciting. At a moment when film or TV versions of novels often end up, at best, as decent airplane watches, opera, as the excellent Lincoln in the Bardo illustrates, has the potential to create something bolder and more bizarre. Opera’s lingering reputation for being stuffy and elitist has helped obscure a fundamental truth about the medium: It’s weird. Even before modern composers started testing the limits of storytelling, operas tended to be guided by minimal logic; if you’d like to feel exceptionally confused, I suggest reading a synopsis of Richard Wagner ’s Tannhäuser . And the form relies on artifice to function. There is nothing naturalistic about characters conversing in song with the kind of vocal power and dexterity that could make a skeptic believe in God. This means that there is effectively no such thing as a shy opera—at least not one that stands the test of time. Any opera that succeeds must quickly teach audiences to understand that what they’re going to experience won’t obey the laws of many other forms of entertainment—the kinds in which plot developments are reasonably justified, characters don’t share their every thought in repetitive and excruciating detail, and the gates of hell don’t suddenly open in a dining-room floor. [ Read: George Saunders has a new mantra ] This makes opera a natural fit for Lincoln in the Bardo , a not-very-realistic novel that’s written almost entirely in dialogue. Saunders’s book is set the night after the burial of President Abraham Lincoln’s 11-year-old son, Willie, and is narrated by more than 150 voices, most of them belonging to Willie’s new neighbors in Oak Hill Cemetery in Washington, D.C. Some become Willie’s spiritual guides: the Reverend Everly Thomas, the frustrated Vollman, and a young gay man named Roger Bevins III. Others are stranger and more profane. Some souls have suffered greatly, most notably the enslaved people buried outside the cemetery boundaries, and some have inflicted suffering, including an enslaver whose streams of pure bigotry are difficult to read. As Thomas, Vollman, and Bevins urge Willie to leave the bardo—a space between life and the afterlife, as defined in Buddhism, that’s dangerous for children—the living Lincoln wanders among them. His grief, more than anything else, is what keeps Willie from moving on to whatever comes next. I’ve been trying to imagine what a Hollywood adaptation of this astonishing tonal chaos could possibly look like. (One is in the works , a hybrid live-action, stop-motion film in which Tom Hanks will play the president.) In recent years, the often risk-averse studio system has favored, with notable exceptions such as the joyously bizarro Poor Things , literary adaptations that hew to basic genre constraints: status-cast thrillers with blockbuster aspirations such as The Housemaid and Verity ; prestige limited series, à la East of Eden , that seem destined to wither away algorithmically as they roll off the Netflix queue; and, as ever, the endless iterations of 19th-century British novels, including the recent Sense and Sensibility and the dubious, upcoming Ebenezer . There remains room, in that milieu, for real artistry, but perhaps not for a choice as wild and possibly alienating as the Met’s X-rated puppet. Without the freedom to be truly outlandish, could an adaptation really do justice to Bardo ? I can’t envision a version of the novel that waters down its most outré choices but also manages to preserve its magic. An opera adaptation of Bardo must, of course, pare back. Many dozens of well-defined characters bounding across the stage would be exciting, but also impractical. Yet it needn’t water down: A successful opera is big, and also strange. That’s especially true now; opera companies including the Met , recognizing the need to attract younger audiences, have put more emphasis on developing new works that can make the old form seem fresh. That shift has seemed to breed greater comfort with challenging choices. Among the many contemporary operas the Met has premiered in recent years are a new version of the myth of Orpheus and Eurydice narrated by three stones—yes, stones—and a harsh, mind-bending adaptation of Luis Buñuel’s surrealist film The Exterminating Angel . Lincoln in the Bardo —the opera—is hugely entertaining. It’s full of apt little musical jokes; the most spiritually harrowing scene, in which Reverend Thomas recounts his journey to the bardo, is repeatedly interrupted by the ludicrous ditties of a “doodling Pennsylvanian.” But the show also embraces, and enhances, many of the most difficult elements of Saunders’s novel. The creators have made the striking decision, for instance, to have a teenage girl named Elise Traynor, who is trapped in the bardo in a state of grisly eternal torment, be portrayed by a male countertenor. The uncanniness of watching an adult man take the guise of a young girl helps make that girl’s plight more visceral. It is a constant reminder, almost below the level of awareness, that Elise will never reach maturity. She won’t have the chance to discover what kind of adult she might be—deep-voiced or dulcet-toned, rebellious or traditional, effeminate or masculine. [ Read: The art of book-to-film adaptations ] That kind of layered creativity represents opera’s literary capabilities at their best. A great book creates a private emotional landscape inside the reader: a kind of internal set piece that contains the characters, the space they occupy, and the feelings they provoke. When I open the book Lincoln in the Bardo , I also travel to the tiny, three-dimensional model of it that lives somewhere between my mind and my heart. Opera, like film, can’t re-create the personal experience of reading; the characters will never look just as you pictured them. But it can create an accentuating mirror to that experience. In my imagined version of Saunders’s bardo, Elise Traynor now has a voice. Because that voice isn’t quite what I expected, I’ve started to think about the character in new, unsettling, enriching ways. Because of the opera, she’s taken on a bit more of a life of her own. The most haunting refrain in Lincoln in the Bardo belongs to young Willie Lincoln. Unsure of where he is and why, and desperate to be reunited with his parents, he invents a credo for how he will get home: “never if weak, maybe if strong.” The audience knows his case is hopeless, but it’s impossible not to be moved by his innocent courage, or by the sweet, mournful instrumentation that accompanies it. His words also function as something like an ethos for the opera itself: To stand a chance at success, it must do the thing with bravery, no holds barred.

items.title: These 5 divisions define how far we can go in space
items.summary: In this Universe, just because you can see it doesn’t mean you can reach it. Conversely, just because you can’t see it today doesn’t necessarily mean that its light won’t arrive tomorrow. Because the fabric of the Universe itself is expanding, and because the maximum speed at which any signal — whether massive or massless — can travel through that fabric of space is finite, there are both: places that we can currently see that we could never reach or communicate with, and places that we cannot currently observe today, but whose light is on the way and will someday reach us in the future. Today, there’s a well-understood limit for how far we can observe in any direction in space: 46.1 billion light-years. That limit is the size of the presently observable Universe, and it’s set by the combination of the initial expansion rate at the start of the hot Big Bang, the matter-and-energy contents of the Universe, the amount of time that’s elapsed since the hot Big Bang occurred, and the value of the maximum signal speed through space: the speed of light. Inside of the presently observable Universe is a smaller region that, if we sent a signal or a spacecraft today, could someday reach objects within that volume: the reachability or communicability limit. Outside of the presently observable Universe is a larger region whose light will someday arrive at our eyes: the future visibility limit. And beyond that limit lies the unobservable Universe, whose true extent is unknown. Here’s what defines those four key regions, and what might change our current ways of thinking. This illustration shows galaxies receding mutually away from one another within the expanding Universe: a consequence of both the Big Bang and the late-time onset of dark energy. Although the expansion has been occurring continuously ever since the Big Bang, the fact that we see the expansion ongoing today doesn’t necessarily mean we can extrapolate everything back to a singular point in space and time in our Universe’s past. Credit : Mark Garlick/Science Photo Library There are several keys to understanding how far we can reach and how far we can see at any point in the history of the Universe, but they all require us to begin with two key concepts: the idea of the expanding Universe and the framework of the hot Big Bang. When most of us think of expansion, we think about something stretching and becoming thinner: like the skin of a balloon that’s being blown up. The Universe isn’t actually like that, however. As space itself expands, nothing about it thins or changes; there’s simply more of it than there was at the beginning. The matter and energy that’s within it can become less dense — keeping the number of particles the same while increasing the volume — but the space itself is no different after expanding than before. What can change, however, is the rate of expansion itself. The rate of expansion is related to the (square root of the) total energy density of space at any given moment. As the Universe expands, the component of energy inherent to space itself (dark energy) remains constant and doesn’t dilute, but the portions that are made of matter and radiation do dilute, getting less dense. As a result, the expansion rate drops as the energy density drops, causing the Universe to expand more and more slowly as time goes on. How matter (top), radiation (middle), and dark energy/inflationary energy (bottom) all evolve with time in an expanding Universe. As the Universe expands, the matter density dilutes, but the radiation also becomes cooler as its wavelengths get stretched to longer, less energetic states. Dark energy’s (or inflationary energy’s) density, on the other hand, will truly remain constant if it behaves as is currently thought: as a form of energy intrinsic to space itself. These three components, together, dictate how the Universe expands at all times from the Big Bang until the present day and beyond. Credit : E. Siegel/Beyond The Galaxy The Big Bang, meanwhile, is normally visualized incorrectly : as a singularity, or the birth of time and space, where all of the matter and energy in the Universe was compressed into a single point. That’s not necessarily true and hasn’t been thought to be the case for over 45 years: since cosmic inflation was first proposed. We now recognize that the Big Bang represents the hot, dense, early state associated with our Universe as-we-know-it in its infancy, but that state was preceded and set up by an earlier state: cosmic inflation , where there was no matter or radiation in the Universe, but only an enormous amount of that relentless energy inherent to space itself. In the aftermath of inflation, the hot Big Bang commenced. The Universe began expanding extremely rapidly, as the density during those early moments was tremendous. As it expanded, however: the density dropped, the kinetic energy of each matter particle and the energy of each radiation particle decreased, causing the Universe to expand more and more slowly as time went on. Eventually, the energy density in the form of radiation drops below the total energy density in the form of matter: a transition that occurs a few thousand years after the Big Bang. Neutral atoms form, gravitation leads to black holes, stars, galaxies, and a cosmic web, and eventually, the matter density drops so low that the energy inherent to space itself — today’s dark energy — becomes the dominant form of energy that determines the expansion of the Universe, a transition which occurred about 6 billion years ago. The relative importance of different energy components in the Universe at various times in the past. Dark matter has been largely important for extremely long cosmic times, and we can see its signatures in even the Universe’s earliest signals. Meanwhile, radiation was dominant for the first ~10,000 years of the Universe after the Big Bang. Note that in the future, when dark energy reaches a number near 100%, the energy density of the Universe (and, therefore, the expansion rate) will remain constant arbitrarily far ahead in time. Credit: E. Siegel Throughout all this time, the amount of Universe that an observer can potentially see has been increasing. We can imagine that, at the onset of the hot Big Bang, from every point in the Universe an enormous amount of omnidirectional radiation emerged. At any other point, you’ll see that initially-emitted light arriving from a spherical surface surrounding you based on the speed of light, the expansion of the Universe, and the amount of time that’s elapsed since the hot Big Bang first occurred. Back when a total time of: 1 picosecond had elapsed, that sphere was about the size of the Earth-Sun distance, 1 millisecond had elapsed, that sphere was about the size of one light-year, 1 second had elapsed, that sphere was about the size of a massive globular cluster, around 20-40 light-years in radius, 1 year had elapsed, the Universe was just a little bit smaller than the radius of the Milky Way, 10,000 years had elapsed, the now matter-dominated Universe was about 10 million light-years in radius, 13.8 billion years had elapsed, bringing us up to our dark energy-dominated present, the Universe is 46.1 billion light-years in radius. It is precisely this line of thinking that leads us to draw conclusions about the size of the observable Universe at any moment in cosmic history: the amount of distance that light generated at the start of the hot Big Bang could have traveled from that event and still reach us. The scale of the Universe (y-axis) versus the age of the Universe (x-axis) on logarithmic scales. Some size and time milestones are marked, as appropriate. Everything contained within the entire observable Universe was once contained in a very small volume, as shown by the size scale on the y-axis. Credit: E. Siegel Howev
